links.note: 432 lists மாணா உவகை, joy without dignity, among a ruler's faults (ஏதம் இறைக்கு); Parimelazhagar glosses it as joy beyond measure. 531 says why such joy is a fault: the சோர்வு (slackness) that comes of சிறந்த உவகை மகிழ்ச்சி is worse than anger beyond measure (இறந்த வெகுளி).

305 says unguarded anger kills the angry person himself (தன்னையே கொல்லுஞ் சினம்). 531 ranks the slackness born of great joy as worse still than excessive anger (இறந்த வெகுளியின் தீதே). Parimelazhagar explains the ranking: anger sometimes destroys enemies too, while this slackness destroys only oneself.

531 states the danger: slackness from the elation of great joy is worse than excessive anger. 539 gives the practice against it: when one grows strong in one's own joy (மகிழ்ச்சியின் மைந்துறும் போழ்து), call to mind those ruined by negligence (இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக).

532 uses as its comparison that constant poverty kills understanding (அறிவினை நிச்ச நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு). 1046 describes one form of it: even when the poor speak good matter well understood, their words and meaning go slack (சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்); Parimelazhagar says nobody listens, so their learning yields nothing. Read together, the 'killing' of understanding in 532 includes its losing all effect in the world.

532 says heedlessness kills fame (பொச்சாப்புக் கொல்லும் புகழை). 601 says the undimmed lamp called family goes out when the grime called sloth creeps over it (மடியென்னும் மாசூர மாய்ந்து கெடும்). In both, an inner lapse, not an outside enemy, destroys a standing built up over time.

533 rests its claim that the heedless have no fame on the settled conclusion of authors of every kind (எப்பால் நூலோர்க்கும் துணிவு). 21 uses the same word for the texts' conclusion about the greatness of renouncers (பனுவல் துணிவு). The pairing shows the Kural appealing to a consensus of books, in the same term, for a rule of statecraft as it does for a claim about ascetics.

534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்ச முடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை). 741 says a fort is of value both to those who march out and to those who, in fear, protect themselves (அஞ்சித் தற்போற்றுபவர்க்கும் பொருள்). The conflict holds if 534's first half is taken as a plain claim about forts and the fearful; Parimelazhagar's readings ease it, since he takes 534 as fear in the mind making a fort useless and 741 as the weaker side prudently taking refuge.

750 says a fort, whatever its excellences, is as nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்). 534 says the fearful have no fort and the heedless have no good (நன்கு). Both hold that an outward advantage counts for nothing without the inner quality needed to use it, and both use the fort to say so.

430 says those without understanding have nothing, whatever they possess (என்னுடைய ரேனும் இலர்). 534 says the heedless have no good (பொச்சாப் புடையார்க்கு நன்கு இல்லை), which Parimelazhagar reads as: even with every kind of wealth, they get no benefit from it. The same logic of having without having is applied to lack of understanding in one verse and to lack of vigilance in the other.

435 says the life of one who does not guard before it comes (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்) perishes like straw before fire. 535 says one who slipped by not guarding beforehand (முன்னுறக் காவாது இழுக்கியான்) will grieve over his own error when the blow lands. The same failure is shown from outside, as destruction, in 435 and from inside, as regret, in 535.

429 gives the positive case: those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) meet no affliction that shakes them. 535 gives the negative: one who did not guard beforehand later grieves over his own fault (தன்பிழை பின்னூறு இரங்கி விடும்). Together they show foresight treated as part of understanding and its absence as heedlessness.

655 tells one not to do deeds over which one will grieve, saying 'what have I done' (எற்றென்று இரங்குவ செய்யற்க). 535 uses the same verb, இரங்கு, for the grief of one who failed to guard in advance. The pairing shows regret following from omission in 535 as it follows from commission in 655.

536 says nothing equals unfailing vigilance toward everyone at all times (யார்மாட்டும் என்றும்). 582 says it is the king's work to know quickly everything that happens to everyone at all times (எல்லார்க்கும் எல்லாம் நிகழ்பவை எஞ்ஞான்றும்). The same universal scope appears in both, and 582 gives the general vigilance of 536 a concrete form in intelligence gathering.

483 asks whether any deed is called hard if one acts with the instruments and knowing the time (கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து செயின்). 537 says nothing is impossible on the ground of being hard if done with the instrument of unforgetting (பொச்சாவாக் கருவியால்). Both use கருவி and the same conditional ending; in 483 Parimelazhagar takes the instruments as outward means, while in 537 he takes the instrument to be the mind itself.

611 says one must not lose heart on the thought that a thing is hard (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை வேண்டும்), since effort gives the greatness needed. 537 says nothing is beyond doing as 'hard' (அரிய என்று ஆகாத இல்லை) when done with unforgetting care. Each denies that difficulty is a reason to give up, and each names its own remedy: effort in 611, sustained attention in 537.

466 says one is ruined by not doing what is fit to do (செய்தக்க செய்யாமை யானுங் கெடும்). 538 says what has been praised must be carefully done, and those who slight it and do not do it (செய்யாது இகழ்ந்தார்க்கு) have nothing through seven births. 538 takes the omission half of 466 and extends its cost beyond this life.

835 says a fool can make, in one birth, the mire he will sink into for seven (எழுமையும் தான்புக் கழுந்தும் அளறு). 538 says those who neglect what is praised have no good through seven births (எழுமையும் இல்). Both attach a seven-birth consequence to conduct in this life, folly in one and neglect of duty in the other.

250 says: when you move against those weaker than you, think of yourself before those stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). 539 says: when you grow strong in your own joy, think of those ruined by negligence (இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக). Both prescribe a deliberate act of recollection at the moment of feeling powerful, for the sake of compassion in 250 and of vigilance in 539.

930 asks whether a drinker, when sober and seeing another man drunk (களித்தானைக் காணுங்கால்), does not reflect on the slackness of his own drinking (உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு). 539 tells one elated with joy to reflect (உள்ளுக) on those whom negligence ruined. Both correct an intoxicated state by looking at its effect in other people, and 930's word சோர்வு is the one 531 uses for the slackness of joy.

666 says people obtain what they thought of just as they thought it, if they are firm (எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப எண்ணியார் திண்ணியர் ஆகப் பெறின்). 540 says it is easy to gain what one thought of if one can keep thinking of it (உள்ளியது உள்ளப் பெறின்). The two have the same structure and the same promise, and differ only in the condition: firmness in action in 666, unbroken attention in 540.

309 says all that one has thought of is gained at once (உள்ளிய தெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்) if one does not think of anger in the heart. 540 says what one thought of is easily gained (உள்ளியது எய்தல் எளிது) if one keeps thinking of it. The shared phrasing sets two conditions for the same result side by side: one thought to be kept out, and one thought to be kept up.

550 says a king's punishing the cruel with death (கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல்) is like weeding the young crop. 551 says a king who takes up harassing people and does wrong is crueller than those who have taken up murder (கொலைமேற்கொண் டாரிற் கொடிதே). The king who may put the cruel to death in 550 is, when he oppresses, placed in 551 below the very people he executes; the two adjacent verses use the same words கொலை and கொடி-.

551 compares the oppressive king to murderers and finds him worse. 552 compares the king who demands wealth to a man standing with a spear saying 'hand it over' (வேலொடு நின்றான் இடுவென்றது). Together the two opening verses of the chapter set the unjust ruler beside common criminals, first the killer and then the robber.

546 says it is not the spear that gives victory but the king's sceptre, if it does not bend (வேலன்று வென்றி தருவது ... கோல்). 552 says the asking of one who stands with the sceptre is like one standing with a spear saying 'give' (வேலொடு நின்றான் ... கோலொடு நின்றான்). The just king's sceptre is set above the spear in 546; in 552 the sceptre used for extortion becomes the spear.

756 names what is the king's wealth: what comes unowned, customs duty, and tribute from enemies (உறுபொருளும் உல்கு பொருளும் தன் ஒன்னார்த் தெறுபொருளும்). 552 treats a sceptre-holder's 'asking' (இரவு) of his people as highway robbery; Parimelazhagar notes that the word இரவு marks it as something other than the due tax. 756 shows the lawful sources against which 552's demand is measured.

520 tells the king to examine daily (நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன்), since if the one doing the work does not bend, the world does not bend. 553 says the king who does not examine daily and do justice (நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்) loses his land day by day. The same wordplay on நாள் and நாடு gives the instruction in 520 and the penalty for ignoring it in 553.

548 says a king who is not easy of access and does not examine and do justice (ஓரா முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்) sinks low and perishes of himself. 553 says a king who does not examine daily and do justice loses his land daily. Both put the failure in not inquiring, not in active cruelty, and both make the ruin follow without any enemy.

381 lists the six things a king must have, among them people and resources (படைகுடி கூழ்...). 554 says a king who bends the sceptre and acts without reflection loses resources and people together (கூழுங் குடியும் ஒருங்கிழக்கும்). The two things injustice costs him in 554 are two of the six that make a king in 381.

568 says the fortune of a king who does not think things through with his circle and then rages in anger will shrink (எண்ணாத வேந்தன் ... சிறுகும் திரு). 554 says a king who acts without reflection (சூழாது) and bends the sceptre loses wealth and people. In both, the king's loss is traced to acting without deliberation, shown in anger in 568 and in injustice in 554.

659 says all that is taken by making others weep goes away with weeping (அழக் கொண்ட எல்லாம் அழப்போம்). 555 says the tears of those who wept, unable to bear their affliction (ஆற்றாது அழுத கண்ணீர்), are the weapon that wears wealth away. 659 states it as a rule for anyone's gains, and 555 applies it to the wealth of an unjust ruler.

828 says a weapon hides within an enemy's folded hands, and his shed tears are the same (படையொடுங்கும் ... அழுத கண்ணீரும் அனைத்து). 555 calls the tears shed by the afflicted the weapon that wears away wealth (அழுத கண்ணீர் ... படை). Both join the same two words, tears and weapon: in 828 the tears conceal a weapon, and in 555 the tears are the weapon.

567 says harsh words and punishment beyond bounds are a file that wears down a king's conquering strength (அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்). 555 says the tears of the afflicted are a tool that wears down wealth (செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). Both describe the effect of a king's cruelty as slow abrasion by a tool, using the same verb தேய்க்கும்.

390 says one who has giving, kindness, a straight sceptre and care of the people is a light to kings (வேந்தர்க் கொளி). 556 says that without just rule the light of kings does not last (மன்னாவாம் மன்னர்க் கொளி). The same closing phrase is used first for what makes a king's lustre and then for what makes it fail, with செங்கோல் named in both.

563 says a king of cruel sceptre who goes on doing what terrifies will certainly and quickly perish (ஒருவந்தம் ஒல்லைக் கெடும்). 556 says kings endure through just rule (மன்னர்க்கு மன்னுதல் செங்கோன்மை) and without it their lustre does not endure. Both tie how long a king lasts to how he rules; Parimelazhagar takes what endures in 556 to be the king's fame.

542 says the whole world lives looking to the sky and the people live looking to the king's sceptre (வானோக்கி வாழும் உலகெல்லாம் மன்னவன் கோல்நோக்கி வாழுங் குடி). 557 says the king's lack of tender care (அளியின்மை) is to the living what lack of rain (துளியின்மை) is to the earth. 557 is the same comparison turned to its negative, and Parimelazhagar refers back to 542 in his comment on it.

In 1192 a woman says that the tender care a lover gives the one who loves him (வீழ்வார் அளிக்கும் அளி) is like the sky giving rain to those who live by it (வாழ்வார்க்கு வானம் பயந்தற்று). 557 says a king's lack of அளி is to living beings what lack of rain is to the earth. The same word அளி and the same rain comparison describe dependence on a ruler in one book and on a beloved in the other.

1041 says that nothing is as painful as poverty except poverty itself (இன்மையின் இன்மையே இன்னாதது). 558 opens with the same words and names something more painful: having (இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை), when one falls under the sceptre of a king who does not do justice. 558 sets a condition on 1041's general claim; Parimelazhagar explains that under a grasping ruler it is the propertied who suffer.

408 says wealth lodged with the unlearned is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (வறுமையின் இன்னாதே கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு). 558 says having is more painful than not having under an unjust king (இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை). Both reverse the usual ranking of wealth over poverty with the same comparative form, because of who holds the wealth in 408 and who rules over it in 558.

545 says rain and harvest come together in the land of a king who wields the sceptre as it should be wielded (பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு). 559 says that if the king bends justice the sky withholds its rain in season (முறைகோடி ... உறைகோடி ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்). The two state one belief from both sides, that rainfall answers to the king's justice.

55 says that when a wife who worships her husband says 'rain', it rains (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). 559 says that when a king bends justice, the sky will not rain (ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்). In both, rain responds to a person's keeping or failing the duty of their station, the wife's in the household and the king's in the realm.

239 says land that bears a body without renown declines in its blameless rich yield (வண்பயன் குன்றும்). 559 says the sky holds back rain when the king bends justice, and the next verse, 560, uses the same verb for cows' yield (ஆபயன் குன்றும்). In each, nature's yield falls in response to a human moral failing, an individual's in 239 and a ruler's in 559.

543 says the king's sceptre stands as the first ground of the brahmins' book and of virtue (அந்தணர் நூற்கும் அறத்திற்கும் ஆதியாய் நின்றது மன்னவன் கோல்). 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, those of the six occupations forget their book (அறுதொழிலோர் நூல்மறப்பர்). 560 shows what 543's claim means in the negative: remove just rule and the learning that depends on it lapses.

134 says that the Veda, even if forgotten, can be learned again, while a brahmin's birth is ruined if conduct declines (மறப்பினும் ஓத்துக் கொளலாகும்). 560 names the forgetting of their book by the men of six occupations (நூல்மறப்பர்) as a sign of a kingdom left unguarded. The same event, forgetting the scripture, is treated as a recoverable personal lapse in 134 and as a mark of public ruin in 560.

19 says that if the sky does not give, giving and austerity will not remain in the wide world (தானம் தவம்இரண்டும் தங்கா). 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, cows' yield declines and the six-occupation men forget their book. In both, religious and learned life depends on a provider, the rain in 19 and the king in 560, and fails when the provider fails.
